food.text: Wheat reached Mesoamerica with the Spanish conquest, which began with the arrival of Hernán Cortés in 1519. The Spanish ate wheat loaf bread while the indigenous population kept eating corn tortillas, creating a divide between wheat-eating and corn-eating cultures.

After the Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire, Spaniards introduced meats from domesticated animals such as beef, pork, chicken, goat and sheep. They also brought dairy products, especially cheese and milk, along with rice, sugar and olive oil.
Cacao beans worked as money in Mesoamerica. The Spanish conquistadors noted in 1545 that thirty beans could buy a small rabbit, one bean a large tomato, and a hundred beans a turkey hen.

The Spanish defeated the Aztec and replaced Tenochtitlán with Mexico City, the capital of New Spain. They planted wheat, installed ovens to bake loaf bread and built a new market without tortillas. Tortillas were restricted to segregated indigenous markets, since the Spanish found them flavorless and believed Europeans were healthiest eating European foods.

Natives of Mexico stayed reliant on maize even under Spanish rule. It was less expensive than the wheat favored by European settlers, easier to cultivate and gave higher yields, even as European control over the land grew stronger with the founding of wheat farms.

According to the earliest documented evidence, chocolate was introduced to the Spanish court in 1544 by Qʼeqchiʼ Mayan nobles brought to Spain by Dominican friars. The first official shipment of cacao to Europe was not recorded until 1585. There is no evidence that Cortés was responsible for its introduction.

Cortés's estate received 1,600 tortillas per week to feed indigenous servants. This shows how tortillas remained the everyday food of indigenous people in the colonial economy, even though the Spanish looked down upon them.
Colonists in Mexico City ate corn tortillas in emergencies, despite their disdain for them. One such emergency was a wheat crop failure in 1602.
Cocoa beans were valuable enough to be counterfeited. Substitutes included dough made of amaranth, wax or broken avocado pits.

In 18th century Mexico City, wheat was baked into leaved rolls called pan francés or pan español, but only two bakers were allowed to make this style, working on consignment to the viceroy and the archbishop. Large ring loaves called pan floreado were available for wealthy Creoles.
Cocoa beans were often counterfeited, with substitutes including dough made of amaranth, wax or broken avocado pits. Royal stores were claimed to hold massive amounts of cocoa beans.

art.text: Colonial Mexican art stayed tied to religion, and most of it went into building and decorating churches. In the eighteenth century, secular art expanded, especially casta paintings, portraiture, and history painting. Almost all of it followed the European tradition, though indigenous elements remained.

Casta paintings, made in eighteenth-century New Spain, depicted a system of racial hierarchy. Each canvas usually showed one idealized family, with a father of one racial category, a mother of another, and children of a third. The genre flourished for about a century and ended with Mexican independence in 1821.

The Spanish Baroque of New Spain is most striking in religious architecture, where indigenous artisans gave it a unique character. Highlights include the Metropolitan Cathedral of Mexico City, the church of Santa Prisca in Taxco, and the Jesuit convent of Tepotzotlan.

Indigenous artists adopted European materials as soon as they became available. In the late 16th century, the Texcocan artist Fernando de Alva Cortés Ixtlilxóchitl painted with ink and watercolor on paper. His portraits of historical Texcocan leaders, bound together in the Codex Ixtlilxóchitl, show shading, modeling and anatomic accuracy.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: The true capital of Mexican Baroque is Puebla. There, an abundance of hand-painted tiles and local gray stone led to a very personal and localized style, with a pronounced Indian flavor.

Lorenzo Rodríguez took Mexican churrigueresque, a fantastically extravagant and visually frenetic ultrabaroque style, to its culmination. His masterpiece is the Sagrario Metropolitano in Mexico City, built between 1749 and 1769.

Between 1684 and 1686, Cristóbal de Villalpando painted huge canvases for the sacristy of the Mexico City Cathedral. They were glued directly onto the walls with arched frames to stabilize them, just under the ceiling vaults. Even the 16th-century fresco work was not usually this large.

Around 1560, Juan Gerson decorated the vault of the Franciscan church in the Nahua town of Tecamachalco with scenes from the Old Testament. Most Nahua artists producing this kind of visual art are anonymous, which makes him an exception.

The Florentine Codex was compiled between 1545 and 1590 by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún. It tells the history of the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire from the Mexica viewpoint. It has bilingual Nahuatl and Spanish text and illustrations by native artists.

The New Spanish Baroque dominated in early colonial Mexico. From the late 17th century to 1750, one of Mexico's most popular architectural styles was Mexican Churrigueresque, which combined Amerindian and Moorish decorative influences.

"Xicochi" is a 17th-century motet written by Gaspar Fernandes while he was organist of Puebla Cathedral. It serves as an example of the influence of indigenous Nahua culture, dominant in Mesoamerica at the time, on colonial Spanish music.
The sanctuary of Ocotlán, begun in 1745, has a surface covered with bright red tiles. These contrast with a plethora of compressed ornament applied generously on the front and sides of its towers.

In 1688, Cristóbal de Villalpando painted the cupola of the Puebla Cathedral, using Rubens' brush techniques. He composed clouds with angels and saints, from which a dove descends to represent the Holy Spirit. The light from the cupola's windows is meant to symbolize God's grace.

Juan Correa, a mulatto artist (1646 to 1716), was a prominent painter of the baroque era. His most famous student, José de Ibarra (1685 to 1756), was also mixed-race. Miguel Cabrera (1695 to 1768), one of Mexico's finest painters, was likely mixed race as well.

Only one known casta painting, by a relatively unknown painter named Luis de Mena, combines castas with Mexico's Virgin of Guadalupe. Some of Mexico's most distinguished artists, including Miguel Cabrera, also painted casta works.

war.text: By 1519 the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world, with an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 people. Its fall in 1521 was a decisive event in the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. The city was almost destroyed by fire and cannon fire. Afterwards Hernán Cortés imprisoned the royal families of the valley and, to prevent another revolt, tortured and killed Cuauhtémoc, the last Aztec Emperor, along with Coanacoch, King of Texcoco, and Tetlepanquetzal, King of Tlacopan.

The Spanish conquest of Yucatán was a much longer campaign than the conquest of central Mexico. It ran from 1551 to 1697 against the Maya peoples of the Yucatán Peninsula and northern Central America. Elsewhere, after the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521, it took decades of warfare to subdue the rest of Mesoamerica, particularly the Mayan regions. The Spanish also used forced labor, often outright slavery, in mining.

Hernán Cortés landed at present-day Veracruz on 22 April 1519, leading a new expedition to Mexico. The Spanish conquest that followed led to the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 and the creation of New Spain. Smallpox began to spread in Mesoamerica immediately after the Europeans arrived. The indigenous peoples had no immunity and eventually died in the millions, with a third of all the natives of the Valley of Mexico dying within six months of the Spaniards' arrival.

The last independent Maya city, Tayasal on Lake Petén Itzá in northern Guatemala, held out against the Spanish until 1697. The Itza at Tayasal and the Kowoj at Zacpeten remained independent long after the Aztecs fell.

On 8 February 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba left Santiago de Cuba to explore the shores of southern Mexico. Many of his men were killed, most during a battle near the town of Champotón against a Maya army. Hernández himself was injured and died a few days after his return to Cuba.

In 1692 a plebeian mob in Mexico City tried to burn down the viceroy's palace and the archbishop's residence. The cause was a hike in maize prices that hit the urban poor, and the rioters shouted, "Kill the Spaniards and the Gachupines who eat our corn!" The article says the punishment that followed was swift and brutal, and no further riots in the capital challenged Spanish rule.

Indigenous resistance in Mexico predates the War of Independence. One example is the 1761 Peasant Revolt in Puebla, a response to colonial policies. Though suppressed, such movements sustained opposition traditions.

Unlike the 1624 riot, in which elites were involved and the viceroy was ousted with no repercussions for the instigators, the 1692 riot was started by plebeians alone. It also had an added racial component. The rioters attacked key symbols of Spanish power and shouted, "Kill the Spaniards and the Gachupines who eat our corn! God wants us to finish off the Spaniards! We do not care if we die without confession!"
In 1799 a small group in Mexico City who wanted independence carried out the Conspiracy of the Machetes. It was an isolated and abortive event that came before the upheaval of 1808.

By the end of the 17th century, it was compulsory to include chocolate in British Navy rations. Cocoa had come to England from Jamaican plantations after Britain conquered the island from Spain in 1655.

Indian auxiliaries in Spanish service needed special permission to carry European arms. Metal swords brought them more prestige than the macuahuitl, in the eyes of Europeans and natives alike, though the auxiliaries commonly used the macuahuitl too.

literature.text: Within twenty years of the Spanish arrival, texts in Nahuatl were being written in the Latin script. Following the conquest, Nahuatl became a literary language, and many chronicles, grammars, poems, administrative documents and codices were written in it during the 16th and 17th centuries.

Spanish friars taught indigenous scribes to write their languages in alphabetic letters after the conquests of the sixteenth century. Many oral histories of the prehispanic period were then recorded in alphabetic texts, while indigenous writers in central and southern Mexico kept producing texts with pictorial elements.

In both Nahuatl and Classic Maya, one word served for both writing and drawing: tlàcuiloa in Nahuatl and tz'iib' in Classic Maya. Pictures were sometimes read phonetically, and texts meant to be read were sometimes very pictorial. This blurred line still makes inscriptions hard for modern scholars to interpret.

Important literary works in Mesoamerican languages include the Popol Vuh and the dance-drama Rabinal Achí, both in Classical Kʼicheʼ Maya. Others are the songs of the Cantares Mexicanos in Classical Nahuatl and the books of Chilam Balam in Yucatec Maya, which hold prophetical and historical accounts.

The first Nahuatl grammar, written by Andrés de Olmos, was published in 1547. That was 3 years before the first grammar in French and 39 years before the first one in English. By 1645, four more had followed, including Horacio Carochi's, now considered the most important colonial-era Nahuatl grammar.

Poems attributed to the philosopher-king Nezahualcoyotl survive mainly in two colonial-era manuscripts, the Cantares Mexicanos and the Romances de los señores de Nueva España. The Cantares was written between 1585 and 1597, but its contents appear copied from lost originals of the 1550s to 1570s, possibly collected by indigenous informants for Bernardino de Sahagún.
tags: Romances de los señores de Nueva España

literature.text: The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco was founded in 1536. It taught both Indigenous and classical European languages to Native Americans and priests. Missionaries there and elsewhere wrote grammars of Indigenous languages for use by priests.
tags: Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

literature.text: Diego de Landa's Relación de las cosas de Yucatán contained Maya calendar signs and a syllabary. Ximenez's manuscript of the Popol Vuh is another early post-Columbian source that preserved indigenous literature.
tags: Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

literature.text: Codex Mendoza, made around 1541, is a mixed pictorial and alphabetic Spanish manuscript. The Dominican Diego Durán, writing before 1581, drew on indigenous pictorials and living informants to create illustrated texts on history and religion.
The Testaments of Culhuacan are a set of sixteenth-century wills bound together as a book. Concentrated in the 1580s, they are the source for a social history of the town.

Since the sixteenth century it has been widely held that Moctezuma II first took Hernán Cortés's 1519 landing for the return of Quetzalcoatl. Ethno-historians question this, noting that the idea appears in no document made independently of Spanish influence. Most such documents are Spanish, like Cortés's letters to Charles V.

The Romances de los señores de Nueva España were preserved with the Relación of Juan Bautista Pomar, which was composed in 1582. The surviving manuscript is believed to be from the 17th century. Pomar, also a descendant of Nezahualcoyotl, may have thought of him as a composer as early as the late 16th century.
tags: Romances de los señores de Nueva España

science.text: Through the 16th century, the Spanish were interested in the medicinal qualities of Mesoamerican plants. Spain during this period viewed chocolate primarily as a medicinal substance rather than a treat.

Francisco Hernández, royal physician to Philip II of Spain, reported to Spain a range of conditions that he believed chocolate and its additives could treat. He and the writer Bernal Díaz also claimed that chocolate was an aphrodisiac.

Motolinia, a 16th-century Spanish observer, left an account of how prismatic obsidian blades were produced. Because he watched the craft being practiced, his description is a key source for modern attempts to redesign the production technique.

Chocolate reached Spain as a medicine. Writers such as Bernal Díaz and Francisco Hernández, the royal physician to Philip II of Spain, claimed it was an aphrodisiac, and Hernández reported to Spain a range of conditions he believed chocolate and its additives could treat. By the mid-16th century it was being manufactured and sold in large quantities, and by the 17th century Madrid had stored around 700,000 pounds of cacao.

politics.text: Between 1519 and 1521, Hernán Cortés and a small European army, joined by a large allied army of Indian auxiliaries, overthrew the most powerful pre-Columbian empire in Mesoamerica. The Aztecs ruled through local rulers, and their power rested on a perception of unchallengeable military supremacy. That made the system unstable and vulnerable to a loss of prestige.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
tags: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

politics.text: In 1546, Spanish authorities discovered silver in the Zacatecas region and set up mining settlements in Chichimeca territory. The Chichimeca resisted by attacking travelers and merchants along the silver roads. The resulting Chichimeca War (1550 to 1590) became the longest and costliest conflict between Spanish forces and indigenous peoples in the Americas.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

politics.text: In 1697, Martín de Ursúa y Arizmendi captured Nojpetén, the island capital of the Itza kingdom, in a Spanish assault on 13 March. With the defeat of the Itza, the last independent and unconquered native kingdom in the Americas fell to European colonisers. About 60,000 Maya were living around Lake Petén Itzá at the time, many of them refugees from other areas. An estimated 88% of the inhabitants died during the first decade of colonial rule. Disease caused most of those deaths, but war between rival Maya groups and Spanish expeditions also took its toll.

Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521 after a siege during which a smallpox epidemic killed thousands. Pedro de Alvarado's destruction of the aqueducts forced the Aztecs to drink lake water, causing disease and thousands more deaths. Spanish and allied attackers massacred 800 civilians in late July, killed 12,000 more on 3 August, and on 12 August massacred many thousands of non-combatants in their shelters. At least 100,000 Aztecs died in the siege. Its fall began Spanish colonial rule in Mexico, and the Viceroyalty of New Spain was established in 1535.

The Aztec Empire began as an alliance of three city-states: Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan. Although it was conceived as an alliance of three self-governed partners, Tenochtitlan became dominant militarily. By the time the Spanish arrived in 1519, the lands of the alliance were effectively ruled from Tenochtitlan, while the other partners had taken subsidiary roles.

In 1585, Don Alvaro Manrique de Zúñiga, Marquis of Villamanrique, became viceroy and was infuriated that some Spanish soldiers were raiding peaceful villages to sell people into slavery. With no military end to the Chichimeca War in sight, he negotiated with Chichimeca leaders and gave them lands and agricultural supplies. This policy of "peace by purchase" finally ended the war.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

politics.text: The territory Cortés conquered became New Spain, headed by a viceroy who answered to the Spanish Crown via the Council of the Indies. The Captaincy General of Guatemala had its capital at Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala. It also covered Chiapas, El Salvador, Honduras and Costa Rica.
tags: Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala

politics.text: In 1523, Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado began the conquest of northern Central America. By 1528 most major Maya kingdoms had been subjugated, though the Petén Basin stayed outside Spanish control.

In 1554, during the Chichimeca War, the Chichimecas attacked a train of sixty wagons on the silver roads. They captured more than 30,000 pesos worth of valuables, inflicting a great loss on the Spanish. By the 1580s, thousands had died and Spanish mining settlements were continually under threat.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

politics.text: In 1624, elites ousted the reformist Viceroy Diego Carrillo de Mendoza, 1st Marquess of Gelves, who had sought to break up crime rackets from which they profited and to curtail opulent displays of clerical power. They stirred up an urban religious riot of Mexico City commoners. The crowd was reported to have shouted "Death to bad government! Death to the heretic Lutheran [Viceroy Gelves]! Arrest the viceroy!" The attack was aimed specifically at Gelves, seen as a bad representative of the crown, not at the monarchy itself.

Before the Spanish conquest, Petén was divided into different Maya polities engaged in a complex web of alliances and enmities. The most important groups around the central lakes were the Itza, the Yalain and the Kowoj. Other groups included the Kejache, the Acala and the Lakandon Chʼol.

Since the sixteenth century, it has been widely held that Moctezuma II believed Cortés's landing in 1519 was Quetzalcoatl's return. Ethno-historians question this, arguing the idea appears only in documents shaped by Spanish influence, such as Cortés's letters to Charles V. In those letters, Cortés presents the Aztecs' gullibility as a great aid to the conquest.

In 1515, Aztec armies commanded by the Tlaxcalan general Tlahuicole invaded the Purépecha Empire once again. The Aztec army failed to take any territory and was mostly restricted to raiding. The Purépecha defeated them and the army withdrew.
Before 1808 upended New Spain's politics, a small group in Mexico City staged an isolated and abortive event in 1799 called the Conspiracy of the Machetes. Its members were seeking independence.

philosophy.text: In the 17th century, Sor Juana Inez de la Cruz emerged as one of Mexico's most prominent early philosophers. A nun, poet, and scholar, she critiqued the societal and religious constraints of her time and advocated for women's education and intellectual freedom.
tags: Sor Juana Inez de la Cruz

philosophy.text: In colonial Mexico the Catholic faith was the only one permitted. Non-Catholics, and Catholics other than Indians, who held unorthodox views were subject to the Mexican Inquisition.

After the fall of Tenōchtitlan in 1521, the Spanish increasingly demanded that altepetl rulers publicly destroy their figures of deities and whitewash temple walls. In Mesoamerican politics, destroying idols had meant a transfer of sovereignty and tributes to the conquering power, but Indigenous peoples soon realized that in the Spanish context it implied a far more sweeping, cosmic transformation. Missionaries and conquistadors also attacked Indigenous priests and adherents on January 1, 1525, destroying the main temples of Tenōchtitlan, Texcoco and Tlaxcala. A letter from Christianized Indigenous nobles to the Spanish crown in 1560 records that people of many altepetl were forced and tortured, hanged or burned because they did not want to relinquish idolatry.

The Diocese of Mexico was created in 1530 and elevated to the Archdiocese of Mexico in 1546, with an archbishop as its head. This gave the Catholic faith, the only one permitted in New Spain, a firm institutional structure.

culture.text: After the Spanish conquests in the sixteenth century, Spanish friars taught indigenous scribes to write their languages in alphabetic texts. Many oral histories of the prehispanic period were recorded this way. Indigenous writers in central and southern Mexico kept producing written texts in the colonial period, many with pictorial elements.

During the 300-year rule by the Spanish, Mexico was a crossroads for the people and cultures of Europe, America and West Africa, with minor influences from parts of Asia. Mexican culture is described as the 'child' of both western and Native American civilizations.

The Popol Vuh is a compendium of Mayan stories and legends, meant to preserve Mayan traditions. Its first known version dates from the 16th century and is written in Quiché with Latin characters. Because it combines historical, mythical and religious elements, it has been called the Mayan Bible.

Since the sixteenth century, it has been widely held that Moctezuma II initially believed Hernán Cortés's 1519 landing to be Quetzalcoatl's return. Ethno-historians question this, noting that most documents expounding the theory are of entirely Spanish origin, such as Cortés's letters to Charles V of Spain.

The Popol Vuh was translated into Spanish by the Dominican priest Francisco Ximénez at the beginning of the 18th century. Its earlier Quiché version had been transcribed in Latin characters, and it remains a vital document for understanding the culture of pre-Columbian America.
The presence of Jews in Mexico dates back to 1521, when Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztecs. He was accompanied by several Conversos.
